item.text:
**Assessment**
Mostly no. I found some limited 2024 inclusion and consultation measures, especially around transitional justice and women’s participation, but the stronger record is repression of opposition regions, minority communities, journalists, and civil-society actors. The positive material is procedural; I found no strong 2024 evidence that Abiy consistently protected political equality in practice.

**Accepted claims**
- **UN Women supports Civil Society Organizations’ engagement in transitional justice policy** | United Nations in Ethiopia | 2024-09-09 | https://ethiopia.un.org/en/283986-un-women-supports-civil-society-organizations%E2%80%99-engagement-transitional-justice-policy  
  Women leaders from NGOs and grassroots groups from multiple regions were brought into the transitional-justice implementation discussion, with an explicit goal of gender sensitivity and women’s participation. This is weak positive evidence for inclusion, but it is a consultation step rather than proof of equal political protection.  
  QIDs: 4B.7, 4B.4

- **EDGE - Enabling Democratic Governance in Ethiopia** | United Nations Development Programme | 2024-01-01 | https://www.undp.org/ethiopia/projects/edge-enabling-democratic-governance-ethiopia  
  UNDP framed a 2024-2027 project around strengthening inclusive, gender-responsive legislative and accountability systems, with explicit attention to women and minority groups claiming rights and participating in democratic decision-making. This is limited positive evidence for institutional inclusion.  
  QIDs: 4B.7, 4B.4

- **Report of the EHRC and OHCHR on community consultations on transitional justice** | Ethiopian Human Rights Commission | 2024-04-08 | https://ehrc.org/download/report-of-the-ethiopian-human-rights-commission-ehrc-and-the-office-of-the-united-nations-high-commissioner-for-human-rights-ohchr-on-the-findings-of-community-consultations-on-transitional-justic/  
  The consultations covered Afar, Amhara, Harari, Oromia, Somali, Tigray, and Dire Dawa, and included women, IDPs, persons with disabilities, traditional/religious leaders, and grassroots CSOs. The design was explicitly described as inclusive, gender-sensitive, and victim-centered. This supports only a narrow positive reading.  
  QIDs: 4B.7, 4B.4

- **Transitional Justice Implementation Roadmap Finalized: Ministry of Justice** | ENA English | 2024-08-19 | https://www.ena.et/web/eng/w/eng_5001231  
  The Justice Ministry said the roadmap would guide implementation and the legal frameworks would create “independent and impartial institutions” for transitional justice. This is a stated institutional commitment, not proof of real-world protection yet.  
  QIDs: 4B.7, 4B.4

- **World Report 2024: Ethiopia** | Human Rights Watch | 2024-01-12 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/ethiopia  
  HRW said the government tightly controlled reporting, detained critical voices, and arrested opposition figures and journalists. It also noted mass arrests of ethnic Amharas, internet/social-media restrictions, and the denial of opposition demonstrations in Tigray. This is strong evidence against protecting unpopular viewpoints and opposition regions.  
  QIDs: 4B.7, 4B.6, 4B.5, 4B.4

- **Ethiopia: Journalist arrested under state of emergency: Belay Manaye** | Amnesty International | 2024-03-14 | https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/afr25/7782/2024/en/  
  Amnesty reported that journalist Belay Manaye was detained under emergency powers for reporting on the Amhara conflict, and that other journalists were also arbitrarily arrested. This is direct evidence against protecting unpopular reporting or political dissent.  
  QIDs: 4B.7, 4B.6, 4B.5

- **The state-of-emergency proclamation centralized coercive authority** | ENA English | 2024-11-03 | https://www.ena.et/web/eng/w/en_30124  
  The proclamation centralized authority under an operation command, allowed replacement of local administrators, restricted CSOs and media suspected of aiding “terrorist” groups, imposed movement/ID controls, and suspended normal judicial handling of enforcement. That is evidence of coercive politicization, not equality protection.  
  QIDs: 4B.7, 4B.5, 4B.6, 4B.4

- **Authorities suspended three rights groups while Abiy praised reforms** | Human Rights Watch | 2024-12-02 | https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/12/02/ethiopia-authorities-suspend-three-rights-groups  
  HRW said the government suspended three rights groups while Abiy publicly praised reforms like media freedom and NGO registration. The operational pattern is selective punishment of independent monitors, not protection of pluralism or equal voice.  
  QIDs: 4B.7, 4B.6, 4B.5, 4B.4

**Search gap**
- I found some evidence of consultation and inclusion on paper, but not strong evidence that Abiy’s government in 2024 actually protected minorities, women, or opposition regions from coercion, detention, or discriminatory emergency measures.
- The best positive items are process-oriented: transitional-justice consultations, a governance project, and a roadmap. They do not show durable equal treatment in practice.
